Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-19803 (score CVSS 9.8).

The Printcart Store – Web to Print Product Designer for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Upload in all versions up to, and including, 2.13.2. This is due to the `nbu_crop_image` AJAX handler accepting a user-supplied `url` parameter that `Nbdesigner_IO::convert_url_to_path()` concatenates onto the uploads base directory without normalizing or stripping `../` sequences, and then deriving both the output directory and output file extension via `pathinfo()` from the same attacker-controlled path — with no `stripImage()` call before `writeImage()` is invoked. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to write attacker-controlled PHP content to arbitrary locations outside the uploads directory, resulting in remote code execution when the written file is subsequently requested. This vulnerability is only exploitable when the `nbdesigner_upload_popup_style` site option is set to `a` (Advanced Upload Popup), which causes the handler to be registered for unauthenticated requests; however, the required `save-design` nonce is printed on the fully public frontend `upload-design-file` page, making it trivially obtainable by any anonymous visitor once that configuration is active.

Score CVSS : 9.8

Type de faiblesse (CWE) : CWE-94

Vulnérabilité critique CVE-2026-93754 (score CVSS 9.8).

The payever – WooCommerce Gateway plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file upload leading to remote code execution in various versions up to, and including, 4.8.0. Three WooCommerce-API callbacks (payever_set_sandbox_api_keys, payever_toggle_subscription, payever_synchronization_incoming) are registered with no authentication, capability check, or nonce, and the upload_image() routine writes a remotely fetched file to the public uploads directory using an attacker-controlled basename() BEFORE validating the file type. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to write an executable PHP file and achieve remote code execution. NOTE: the token-recovery leg of the full chain depends on the plugin's outbound validateToken() call to Payever's service; the unauthenticated hard-coded-credential identity overwrite (CWE-862/CWE-798) is independently exploitable.

Score CVSS : 9.8

Instance snapshots ignore the restricted.containers.lowlevel=block setting; allowing for arbitrary command execution on the Incus server by abusing lowlevel hooks such as raw.lxc and raw.qemu .

As snapshots can be moved from one server to another, a malicious instance+snapshot can be crafted locally, moved to a restricted project and the snapshot restored for arbitrary command execution.

Attaque Mis à jour le 6 novembre 2026 à 7h15 Pharmagest : une faille de sécurité pourrait exposer les données de patients de milliers de pharmacies françaises Une possible faille de sécurité touchant les logiciels Pharmagest, utilisés dans des milliers de pharmacies françaises, soulève de sérieuses interrogations sur la protection des données des patients. Selon des signalements rendus publics le 5 novembre 2026, certains ordinateurs équipés de ces solutions pourraient être accessibles à distance par l’intermédiaire d’un serveur VNC insuffisamment sécurisé. Le problème serait particulièrement préoccupant : le mot de passe permettant de se connecter correspondrait au nom d’hôte de la machine, autrement dit à son propre identifiant informatique. Plus inquiétant encore, cette faiblesse aurait déjà été signalée à l’éditeur en septembre 2025, soit près de quatorze mois auparavant. Incident de sécurité rapporté par The Record.

DigiCert explained that over the summer, an internal business system was "externally accessible when that was not intended," and someone had created an unauthorized account.

Internet security firm DigiCert reported a data breach involving an internal business system that was left exposed and eventually accessed by someone outside of the company.

The Utah-based company did not respond to requests for comment but posted a lengthy post-mortem on Mozilla's Bugzilla platform explaining the situation.

DigiCert, which is a certificate authority and offers other corporate security services, said the incident began in February 2025 when an internal business system was moved out of a VPN-restricted network, making it accessible externally. Certificates typically help to verify the security of web servers.

“Beginning on 2026-06-21, DigiCert determined that the business system was externally accessible when that was not intended, and that an unassigned account had been created,” the company said, adding that the issue was fixed by July 2.

On October 19, DigiCert confirmed that the database was accessed starting on June 27 and that it was a “reportable event.” The accessed data included customer names, business email addresses, phone numbers as well as documents like driver’s licenses, passports or utility bills and other info.

A spokesperson for the company declined to say whether the attackers have contacted DigiCert, telling Recorded Future News that they are “focused on providing our customers with information relevant to them about the incident.”

Signal de veille — The Record.

Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, is facing up to 20 years in prison on wire fraud and money laundering charges after admitting to using his position on an FBI investigative squad to steal more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency to cover his debts.

A senior FBI official pleaded guilty to stealing millions in cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by nation-state hackers and theft victims.

Yaroch was an FBI Supervisory Special Agent who worked at FBI Headquarters within the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division — with his work focusing on an unnamed nation-state.

He used his seniority to access FBI systems that had the codes and passwords necessary to take cryptocurrency from at least two adversarial nations as well as 10 victims of crimes. In total, he conducted 100 transfers from 79 wallets starting in December 2024. The wallets were connected to 35 different FBI investigations.

Yaroch had hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit card debt, loans and car payments. He paid off several large loans. The Justice Department gained access to his ChatGPT conversations, which showed he planned to buy a vineyard in Portugal and retire.

Yaroch began to make legal arrangements in Portugal and bought plane tickets to the country for him, his wife and his child slated for September. But he ended up confessing to the theft to a DOJ employee in July.

Yaroch told the DOJ employee, who he knew from a previous job, that he was angry about an investigation of a suspect from an unnamed adversarial nation. Yaroch "became frustrated when he could not do more to disrupt this individual's use of cryptocurrency.”

This is fascinating : The video describes a technique that can reveal where an otherwise unidentifiable recording was made by analyzing its audio for the faint sounds of passing aircraft. The technique is both fascinating and frightening. It works by looking at Doppler curves, which plot the way a plane’s sound changes as it passes overhead because of the Doppler effect. This is the same familiar Doppler effect that causes the frequency of a siren to rise as it approaches and then fall as it passes by and moves away. More generally, it’s the phenomenon whereby the frequency of a wave perceived by an observer changes when the observer and the source of the wave are moving in relation to one another. […] It’s sound that’s relevant here, though, and specifically the sound of aeroplanes. Early in his video, Colsto brings up a map of the flights that were in the air at the time the video he’s tracing was recorded. Much of this information is publicly available. Aircraft equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast (ADS-B) transmit data about their position, velocity, and altitude, which flight-tracking services collect and make available to the public. While not every plane is tracked, the system provides an enormous amount of information about aircraft movements.

The use of a new AI-powered offensive security tool by cyber threat actors appears to be spreading well beyond the campaigns first identified.

This tool, called ARTEX, is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘ Autumn-27 ’ in July 2026.

While ARTEX has already been integrated in several known malicious campaigns since October, a new report by internet traffic scan provider Censys estimated its use could be much more widespread than previously thought.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

In October, two threat intelligence companies attributed its use as part of threat actor operations.

First, in early October, CrowdStrike linked ARTEX to a campaign against South Korean financial institutions . The analysts found ARTEX was used alongside Anthropic’s Claude AI model during the campaign, which ran from late September to early October 2026. CrowdStrike assessed with moderate confidence that the attacker is a Chinese speaker and financially motivated.

Signal de veille — Infosecurity Mag.

BlackFog found a lack of visibility into data being shared with AI tools, even those approved for use in the enterprise

Around half (47%) of security leaders have experienced sensitive data exposure through an AI tool at their organization, research by BlackFog has found.

The researchers said the findings demonstrate that many organizations lack visibility into the types of data being shared with AI tools, even those that are approved for use in the enterprise.

While 62% of respondents could identify users or departments sending data to AI tools, less than half (48%) said they could provide any record of the types of data that had left the organization through AI tools.

“This shows why security teams cannot stop at deciding which AI tools employees are allowed to use. Organizations also need to control what information is shared with them," commented Darren Williams, founder and CEO of BlackFog.

Almost all organizations (98%) reported having an AI usage policy in place. However, the ability to enforce such policies varied significantly.

Just over half (56%) support their broader AI usage policies with comprehensive technical controls. Around a third (35%) said that while their organization has a written policy specifying what information employees must not enter into AI prompts, there is no technical enforcement.

Un système valable sur architecture MoE Le mécanisme permet de démontrer qu’une réponse est bien le résultat du calcul d’un modèle donné, sans en révéler les poids. Le serveur génère d’abord un « engagement » ; c’est-à-dire une empreinte qui dit son choix exact de poids. Il produit ensuite, sur demande d’un client, un fichier de preuve. Anthropic communique des performances pour une configuration bien spécifique. Dans les grandes lignes : Modèle MoE (Llama 4 Maverick) quantifié en 4 bits Serveur à 1 GPU H100 et 24 cœurs CPU Séquences d’output de 1024 tokens traitées par lots de 24 La génération de l’empreinte cryptographique initiale prend à peu près 39 minutes. Cette empreinte pèse quelques Mo. Elle est réutilisable sur environ 16 millions de requêtes avant qu’on doive la recalculer. Le débit de génération des preuves avoisine 110 tokens par seconde.
